#1102. Tuchel: Bellingham and I were up and down – now we are in a good place

England head coach Thomas Tuchel described his relationship with Jude Bellingham as being “in a good place” after admitting it had been “a bit up and down”.

Tuchel has two Bellinghams in his latest England squad after calling up Jude’s brother, Jobe, for the first time for the Nations League games against Croatia and Spain. If they play together, it will be the first time brothers have represented England in the same team since Gary and Phil Neville 19 years ago.

This time last year, Tuchel cast doubt over Jude’s place in his team by picking Morgan Rogers over him, having not included the Real Madrid midfielder in an England squad the previous month.

But Jude performed superbly for Tuchel at the World Cup and was England’s best player during the last international camp. Tuchel revealed he has listened to his advice by calling up 21-year-old Jobe.

Asked if his relationship with Jude has developed, Tuchel said: “It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course, but we are in a good place.

“I love to be his coach, he’s a top player, a very influential player and it goes both ways. If Jude was not feeling comfortable, he would not perform at that level.

“At the moment, you see he’s happy to come into camp, he’s happy with the role he has, he’s fully invested and now to have the chance to have both of them [Bellingham brothers] is just the next step. I hope we have finished with the down. You never know as a coach.”

Jobe has captained England’s Under-21s and, as well as U21 head coach Lee Carlsey, Tuchel acknowledged the influence of Jude on the Borussia Dortmund midfielder’s first senior call.

Jude once said that playing with Jobe for England would be “the biggest dream of my life” and that it would mean more to him than any trophies.

Discussing Jude’s influence on Jobe’s selection, Tuchel said: “We spoke about his brother because I was aware it was always his dream and Jude was always like, ‘Watch him, he’s good, he can make it,’ I would say, ‘Yeah we are watching him.’ And we know, of course, from Lee Carsley and we see him with the Under-21s and there is such positive feedback.

“This is also the signal that if you are good in the Under-21s, this is the next step. We had it with Elliot Anderson, we had it with Alex Scott, we have it with Jarell Quansah and it counts. If you play good for England in the Under-19s, 20s, 21s, if you play good for England in tournaments then it means something.”

Tuchel at one point had to correct himself, with a laugh, when he accidentally referred to Jobe as Jube. On the subject of how Jobe reacted to his call-up and the comparisons with his brother that he will inevitably face, Tuchel said: “He has to live with this that everyone will compare them. They look similar, even in their movements, but they are very different players. And let’s see – they are also different characters, at least that’s what I heard.

“He [Jobe] watched training very early in my [reign]. In my first March camp maybe, he came over and watched his brother train. We chatted and we said, ‘Ah, it would be nice if one day you are with him [Jude].’ He was very kind and polite and I’m glad to have him in camp.

“He couldn’t stop smiling [when I told him]. He has the same beautiful smile as Jude, so it’s nice to have him. Let’s see what the effect is. What I saw, Jude was always the big brother that you imagine, taking care of his younger brother and making sure everything is alright. Behaving like a big brother. And that helps Jobe now. And it will be beautiful for Jude to have his brother close and in camp and to have this experience together. It’s a very special moment for them.”

The Bellingham name, made famous by his brother Jude, who played for Dortmund from 2020 to 2023 before moving to Real Madrid for almost €130m (£108m), is arguably the most recognisable in Dortmund’s squad. When the club embarked on a marketing tour of Asia last summer, Bellingham was front and centre. At a Puma event in Osaka, he addressed the guests. In Tokyo, where the Dortmund delegation travelled next, a film about BVB was projected on to a huge skyscraper. The central figure: Jobe Bellingham. And after the public training sessions, Japanese supporters were particularly eager to get photos with him.

Jobe never wanted to be a carbon copy of his brother. He wanted to write his own story. The club, too, has resisted direct comparisons. They just wanted Jobe, not the younger brother of a world-class star. Now the brothers will be reunited in the England squad. For Jude, it is a dream come true. He previously said: “We’ve played together on the streets for so long. Playing for England alongside my brother would be the greatest dream of my life. That would mean more to me than any trophy.”

Dortmund have never fought harder for a player in recent years than Bellingham. The club’s executives first met him in person in the summer of 2020, when Jude signed. Jobe accompanied his brother to Germany. From that moment on, the club monitored every step of his development: his progress through the youth ranks at Birmingham City, the family club of the Bellinghams, and the evolution of his positioning on the pitch. After all, as a child, Jobe was still playing as a centre-forward. Over time, however, he gradually moved into deeper roles.

In May 2025, BVB decided to make their move. Word had reached Dortmund that Eintracht Frankfurt were interested and had already invited Bellingham to their training facilities. The pressure was on. Dortmund responded by pulling out all the stops. President Hans-Joachim Watzke, the man who shaped the club for more than two decades and led it to the top of German football, stepped in. He flew to England and met Bellingham face to face. It was a secret mission. Watzke was determined not to attract any attention that could jeopardise negotiations.

The problem: Sunderland, Bellingham’s former club, had secured promotion to the Premier League only a day earlier. Hundreds of supporters were gathered outside the hotel where Watzke and Bellingham were due to meet. To avoid being recognised, Watzke put on sunglasses and a cap before making his way through the crowd. He brought two gifts with him. Firstly, a BVB shirt with Jobe’s name on the back. Secondly, a handwritten note from Kovac expressing his desire to work with the midfielder. A few days later, Watzke received a phone call. It was Jobe. His decision had been made. He was joining Dortmund.

Ever since, the midfielder has enjoyed almost unwavering support. Watzke frequently spoke with him throughout his first season, offering encouragement and reassurance. The same was true of Kovac and other senior figures. Equally important to his breakthrough has been team-mate Felix Nmecha, with whom Bellingham has developed a close friendship and who has become an important source of advice. When time allows, the two enjoy playing padel together. Off the pitch they are opponents; on it they form a midfield partnership.

And while his father Mark was still complaining to club officials around a year ago that his son was not getting enough playing time, the situation has changed dramatically. The Bellingham family are delighted, and his England call-up has provided further confirmation that he is on the right path.

#1101. Heysel ’85 is the definitive, eye-opening drama that finally looks past Liverpool terrace narrative

FourFourTwo attended the 2026 London Film Festival for the screening of 'Heysel 85', which will be released in cinemas this November

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the past 40 years, the tragedy of the 1985 European Cup final has often been reduced in mainstream British discourse to a single, monolithic headline: football hooliganism.

In Heysel ’85, director Teodora Mihai bypasses the familiar cliches of terrace culture to produce something which seeks to change the conversation surrounding the disaster. Coming from a documentary background, Mihai approaches the disaster not as a reflection of senseless violence, but as a study into institutional breakdown and the callous, self-preserving instincts of political power.

The film anchors its narrative through two parallel viewpoints. The principal perspective belongs to Marie Dumont (Violet Braeckman), the fictional press attaché and daughter to the Mayor of Brussels.

Braeckman, a polyglot who learned Italian specifically for the production, delivers a performance of quiet, escalating dread as she watches the veneer of civic competence crumble from within.

Operating on the other side of the crisis is Luca Rossi (Matteo Simoni), an Italian broadcast journalist reporting live from the ground while desperately trying to locate his father, uncle, and brother, all attending the match as Juventus supporters.

Early on, Mihai builds tension through procedural unease. Disorienting, fluid tracking shots wind through subterranean corridors, establishing a sense of foreboding long before the tragic events unfold. Shot in an empty hospital in Antwerp, the oppressive concrete hallways reflect the popular view that the Heysel Stadium, built in 1930, was run-down and unfit for a fixture of such magnitude by the mid-1980s, something which is referenced in the film.

The film avoids the trap of laying blame at the feet of ticket touts, generic mobs, or rowdy Liverpool supporters. It is deeply sympathetic to the ordinary fans caught up in the events of May 29, 1985, casting a forensic eye upward at the organisers.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

UEFA executives, the local municipal government, and a fractured security apparatus are all painted in an unflattering light. The territorial friction between the municipal police and the Belgian Gendarmerie is laid bare; their reluctance and inability to share intelligence or coordinate chain-of-command turns an already combustible situation into an avoidable tragedy.

Nowhere is this administrative failure more grotesque than in the depiction of the Mayor of Brussels (played by Josse De Pauw). Portrayed as a sozzled, cowardly executive, his characterisation is rooted in historical reality. According to Braeckman, De Pauw knew the real-life mayor Hervé Brouhon, a figure regarding whom it was openly joked in local political circles that any serious decisions had to be made before 11am.

The film captures the hollow facade of authority dissipating in direct proportion to his alcohol intake. In one particularly telling sequence early on, Marie is dispatched to fetch the key to the stadium’s liquor cabinet so the mayor and his dignitaries can enjoy a proper drink. It is a bitterly ironic snapshot of municipal priorities just hours before 39 people would lose their lives.

When catastrophe strikes, the narrative strips away any remaining shred of civil propriety. Mihai’s documentary sensibilities ensure the integration of genuine, unaltered archive footage feels seamless rather than exploitative, anchoring the fictional protagonists in historical reality. While the Italian delegation emerges with a degree of grace and anguish, UEFA and local authorities retreat into corporate damage control, consumed entirely by liability, protocol, and the insistence that the match must still be played.

By refusing to take the easy narrative route of sensationalising terrace thuggery, Heysel ’85 delivers an important, unsettling reassessment of the catastrophe. It is an indictment of systemic cowardice that proves human lives were not lost merely to crowd surges, but to the arrogance of an establishment that abdicated responsibility long before kick-off - and, tellingly, never resigned in its wake.

Following its UK premiere at the 70th BFI London Film Festival, Heysel ’85 will be released in UK cinemas on 20 November 2026, distributed by Icon Film Distribution.

#1100. Record-breaking Harry Kane belongs in the company of greats that he keeps. There is only one gap in his record now and he remains as central to ending 60 years of hurt than he has ever been, writes OLIVER HOLT

Published: 16:54 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 20:17 EST, 12 November 2026

Only giants have trodden the path that Harry Kane walked at Wembley on Thursday when he strode out on to the pitch on a bitterly cold winter night, his four young children by his side, and beheld the array of trophies, honours, adulation and respect that awaited him.

It is just 16 days since Kane held his hands to his face, climbed up to the stage at the London Palladium and said 'wow' when Ronaldo 'Il Fenomeno' presented him with the Ballon d'Or trophy that anointed him the best player in the world.

Now, it sat before him on a plinth and Kane broke away from the England line-up and walked forward to hoist it aloft. He showed it to all the corners of the stadium and for a moment, it was framed against the giant tifo bearing his image and the words 'England's Finest' that towered over one end of the ground.

But the Ballon d’Or is old news in the flood of honours that is coming Kane’s way in this golden summer of a great career. Kane had become the first Englishman to win the Ballon d’Or for a quarter of a century and on Thursday night he was to break the 37-year-old record held by Peter Shilton for the most England caps. He scored the winner, too. Of course, he did.

The occasion of England-Croatia in the Nations League was Kane's 126th appearance in an England shirt and Shilton stepped forward to hand him a small case containing a crest to mark the achievement. Finally, the Prince of Wales showed his appreciation to the England captain by presenting him with a commemorative shirt with 'Kane 126' emblazoned on it.

It was a night to feel the weight of football's history and the ghosts of greatness that people England's heritage. Kane belongs in the company he now keeps. He belongs in the pantheon of the game because he is one of the deadliest strikers in history. He belongs in the pantheon because of the humility he has shown and the dedication he devotes to improvement.

Harry Kane celebrated his record-breaking England appearance with a finely struck penalty

Before kick-off, Kane's history-making was celebrated with a commemorative shirt by the Prince of Wales

England (4-2-3-1): Pickford 6; Alexander-Arnold 6 (White 78, 6), Quansah 4, Burn 6, Hall 7; Rice 5 (Garner 78, 5), Anderson 6; Rogers 8, Bellingham 6, Gordon 5 (Ngumoha 78, 5); Kane 7

Croatia (4-2-3-1): Livakovic 5; Smolcic 6 (Marco Pasalic 76 5), Stanisic 6, Vuskovic 6, Gvardiol 5; Misic 5 (Modric 76, 6), Kovacic 6; Sucic 7 (Mario Pasalic 70, 5), Baturina 6, Vlasic 5; Matanovic 5 (Budimir 70, 5)

He belongs with Billy Wright, the first England player to 100 caps, and the man who set the England appearance record at 105 when he played for his country for the last time in 1959. He belongs with Bobby Charlton, who made it to 106 before the heartbreak of the 1970 World Cup quarter-final defeat to West Germany brought his international career to an end.

Kane belongs with Bobby Moore, Charlton's rival as the greatest England player of all time, who reached the new mark of 108 caps in November 1973. That was one of the great numbers in English sport until Peter Shilton finally surpassed it. He reached 125 caps by the time he played his last game for England in the third-place play-off at the 1990 World Cup.

It is quite some lineage. And now it is Kane who holds the prize. And if this was hardly a momentous match, it was a momentous occasion. If you are tired of glorying in a player like Kane, a relentless striker, a wonderful passer, the sweetest striker of the ball you will ever see, a player of vision, a man who exudes the beauty of simplicity and the wonder of modesty, then you are tired of football.

The honours are rushing at him in a giddy, babbling flood. It may be that he reaches close to 200 caps before he retires and even if it already seems likely that that record will be broken by Jude Bellingham, who has 61 caps at the age of 23, Kane's England goals tally, which stands at 92 after another goal against Croatia, will not be under threat for a generation or longer.

The gap, of course, is a tournament victory. That is what still separates Moore and Charlton from him. Kane is a dream of a player but he has not won the World Cup or the European Championship. What remains is the hope that he will put that right in the years that he has left in the game.

Winning the Nations League would not be quite the same but it would be a start and this victory over Croatia took England a small step closer to that goal. A convincing win over Spain in Madrid on Sunday would take them closer to their aim of finishing top of this group and getting a favourable draw in the quarter-finals in the spring.

Kane made his England debut in March 2015 when he was 21 and England's future looks brighter now than it did when he broke through. More than an hour before the game, the men who will follow Kane and perhaps even chase his caps record, chatted animatedly on the pitch. Bellingham, Morgan Rogers, Anthony Gordon and Morgan Gibbs-White are the new breed.

Morgan Rogers opened the scoring inside the opening half-an-hour and celebrated with his trademark cold celebration

England had found themselves pegged back by Croatia after slopping defending drew the visitors level

Referee Morten Krogh was summoned to the monitor to review the penalty shout on Thursday

Kane returned to Wembley triumphant for the first time since his historic Ballon d'Or win

After the Kane festivities, the first half was an anti-climax. Twenty-four minutes of relative drudgery ensued before Kane exhibited the breadth of his talent once again to help put England ahead. He got the ball 30 yards out, looked up and drifted a beautiful diagonal pass out to the right and into the path of Bellingham. Bellingham volleyed it across goal and Rogers forced it over the line.

The second half began slowly, too, but 15 minutes into it, Croatia equalised. England failed to clear a corner, Jarell Quansah tried to head the ball back to Jordan Pickford and, as Kane watched on, Petar Sucic stole in and hooked the ball past the England goalkeeper into the roof of the net.

Quansah made some kind of amends three minutes later when he was dragged down in the box and Danish referee Morten Krogh awarded a penalty. It was Kane-time again. Kane took the kick and lifted it gently and with a touch of curl down the centre of the goal. Dominic Livakovic dived to his left and the ball sailed softly over his trailing leg and into the net.

Croatia had chances to draw level but could not take them. England made changes and young Rio Ngumoha, a winger of rare talent, another with a rich future ahead of him, another who will help to fill the void when the day comes for Kane to bid farewell to England, came on as a late substitute for Gordon.

And so Kane's night of history began to draw to a close. In a 2-1 victory, he had made one and scored one. He remains as central to England's hopes of ending more than 60 years without a trophy as he ever has been. In a career that has festooned him with garlands and left no one in doubt of his greatness, it is the only gap that remains.

Harry Kane has set his sights firmly on rapidly reaching a century of international goals after becoming England’s most-capped player of all time.

The England skipper marked his 126th appearance for the Three Lions with the winner against Croatia in the Nations League – his first goal since picking up the Ballon d’Or last month.

Kane was afforded an emotional presentation pre-match at Wembley to mark both achievements and is already thinking of creating more history after moving within eight goals of a ton.

‘It’s achievable,’ Kane said. ‘I’m getting closer. Breaking the appearance record is a massive thing in the history of our game, seeing the tifo at the stadium and having my kids with me was beyond dreams.

‘It’s important to recognise our great players. It’s maybe something we haven’t done so well over the years with some of our other greats.

‘It's been a crazy few weeks. I don’t know if I’ve fully taken it all in. The reception has been overwhelming.

‘Maybe during the winter break I’ll be on a beach reflecting on everything I’ve achieved, having a drink with my wife.’

Croatia legend Luka Modric, 41, was part of the presentations ahead of kick off and Kane did not rule out attempting to prolong his career in a similar vein to the AC Milan midfielder.

‘He’s an inspiration for a lot of us,’ Kane added. ‘An incredible player and a great person, he’s looked after himself and still to be playing at this level is inspiring for me to push the limits. To see where your body and mentality takes you.

‘As long as I feel I can help, I’ll be here for as long as I can. If that’s until I’m 40, we’ll wait and see.’

Now qualified for the quarter-finals, England need to beat Spain in Madrid on Sunday to top their group and Thomas Tuchel believes they can topple the world champions.

‘It’s a completely different scenario, completely different setup,’ Tuchel said. ‘But I'm very positive that we will get what we want.’

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta has been given a massive boost of three agreements all set to be signed.

The Gunners entered the season somewhat uncertainly with a squad that had lost the likes of Gabriel Martinelli, Leandro Trossard and Gabriel Jesus in attack – but after 10 Premier League fixtures, the champions are at the top of the table, five points clear, with nine of their 10 matches won.

His absence remains keenly felt, with another transfer oversight at the club adding to the challenge they face without him

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester City, what is going on? If you block out the noise, it’s pretty straightforward. They sold Rodri, and they didn’t sign any full-backs.

That’s not the consensus. Sloppy defensive mistakes have critics suggesting players are losing focus, while Enzo Maresca’s post-game comments after City’s third straight Premier League defeat did nothing to quieten the murmurs that the guilty verdict is beginning to gnaw away at his team.

“Today I think [the problem] has been general,” Maresca said. “You need desire and intensity to win second balls and duels; you require intensity, or you struggle - and we didn’t match their intensity.”

But Maresca is wrong - and so are the pundits claiming psychology is the root of City’s drop-off.

Yes, it’s still all about Rodri. We might be tired of saying it but that doesn’t make it any less true.

During his seven years at the club, Manchester City’s win ratio was 71.5% with Rodri and 62.3% without, losing 12.1% of games he played and 26.2% of games he didn’t.

His absence remains keenly felt and never more obviously than on Saturday, because he would have prevented all three Nottingham Forest goals.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

City lack control in possession and are therefore vulnerable to clumsily giving the ball away and conceding high-quality chances, because they don’t have Rodri’s immaculate positioning or smart press-releasing passing around the corner. The way Forest pressed high from the outset tells us Oliver Glasner was well aware of this flaw.

It led to Aston Villa’s opener in the 2-1 defeat, when the ball was spread out to Marc Guehi – who miscontrolled a tough ball – because there was no Rodri-pass in the middle; then it happened again for the opener on Saturday, this time far more egregiously as Elliot Anderson quite literally turned his back on the play.

Anderson was unavailable for the first pass, which would have drawn in the Forest players and opened up a pass out wide, and was unavailable for the second pass, when Josko Gvardiol needed help:

The second and third Forest goals both resulted from missed interceptions by Anderson, who misjudged the move and anticipated the counter too slowly. It is difficult to imagine Rodri making either mistake:

Maresca’s possession football would look more controlled if he had Rodri (or, as at Chelsea, Moises Caicedo) offering a metronomic presence on and off the ball, helping build slowly out from the back while screening against counter-attacks.

And Maresca would have more control with actual full-backs on the pitch. The Rodri Problem is well documented, but rarely have Manchester City been called out for bizarrely deprioritising full-backs, a position Maresca has developed more than any other Premier League manager in recent times.

The way he deployed Marc Cucurella, Reece James, and Malo Gusto – often in multiple positions at once, switching seamlessly depending on the phase of play – was truly innovative, yet he arrived at City without specialists at left-back or right-back.

Gvardiol’s mistake for Forest’s opener probably would not have been made by Cucurella, while Gusto or James would have connected where Matheus Nunes swiped at the air ahead of Brighton’s winner. Moreover, in Maresca’s system proper full-backs would drift neatly into central midfield, covering the very gaps Anderson failed to control on Saturday.

It’s worth noting that City haven’t won the title since Pep Guardiola stopped playing at least one traditional full-back; Kyle Walker or Joao Cancelo (or both) were prominent in each of City’s four in a row.

Losing Rodri and failing to replace him has undermined Maresca. Failing to sign any full-backs has made a difficult task almost impossible.

Alex Keble is a freelance football journalist based in London, specialising in tactical analysis. He has written for BBC Sport, Goal, The Mirror, The Independent, Football 365, and many others. As well as covering Premier League football, Alex works as a child therapist.

#1097. How I balance my life as a professional surfer and a university researcher

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Cliff Kapono is a professional surfer and marine conservation scientist.

Cliff Kapono enjoys professional surfing as an adjunct to his academic career. Credit: Nani Welch Keliihoomalu for Nature

During my graduate studies at the University of California, San Diego, long hours in the laboratory were often stressful, and not just because of the research. Most of my anxiety came from looking out the window at perfect surfing conditions and realizing I didn’t have much time to finish my experiments and leave while the ‘waves were firing’.

Several years on, I am now an assistant professor at the School of Ocean Futures at Arizona State University (ASU), working from Hilo, Hawaii, where I balance scientific research with my second job: travelling the world as a non-competitive professional surfer. Also known as a free surfer, I ride a variety of board designs — from conventional wooden surfboards to modern big-wave ‘guns’ — and produce social-media content, such as photos and videos, in exchange for endorsement opportunities.

My research is also deeply connected to the ocean. I study coral microbiomes, sampling the community of microorganisms living on and in the coral before and after environmental stress to improve understanding of reef health and the sea-bed formations that create waves, referred to as surf breaks. In May, my colleagues and I reported on the importance of creating a framework to analyse systems with environmental, social and cultural components to protect surf ecosystems1.

In my faculty position, I work in nine-month appointments, and I am permitted to spend a number of work hours each calendar year on non-conflicting outside business. I spend roughly 85% of my work year on research and teaching and 15% on surfing assignments.

Many careers are no longer confined to a single discipline or identity, and some of the most meaningful work now happens at the intersection between different skills, communities and ways of thinking. Surfing shapes the questions I want to ask as a scientist, while science provides me with ways to understand and protect ocean environments. When I was a student, I used to worry that I would have to choose between surfing and science. Today, my career exists because I didn’t.

When I graduated from high school in 2005, Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders made up less than 0.2% of all science, technology, engineering and mathematics degree graduates in the United States. Today, that number remains at only 0.3%2. As a Native Hawaiian kid, targeted fellowships and private programmes made university possible for me, covering my tuition and board.

After I started a PhD chemistry programme at the University of California, San Diego, in 2012, my studies became much more demanding. Courses, a teaching-assistant role, fellowship requirements and lab training would keep me on land from sunrise until sundown. Despite being able to see the ocean from nearly every window on campus, it was the time in my life that I felt furthest from it.

Remarkably, it was during the third year of my PhD programme that getting paid to surf actually became a reality. After many nights spent in the lab, I decided to set academic boundaries and rededicate time to the waves, mostly as a way to protect my mental health. I stopped measuring success only by hours in the lab. Instead, I treated time in the ocean as part of the scientific process.

Can a 'lullaby' save coral reefs from extinction?

Can a 'lullaby' save coral reefs from extinction?

Surfing-industry figures took notice, and not long after becoming more present on the beaches, I was offered modest ambassadorial contracts that developed into respectable budgets that let me travel to places with better waves and to collaborate with local board builders — when not in the lab, of course.

When I moved back to Hawaii in 2018, I received a US National Science Foundation postdoctoral fellowship for broadening participation of under-represented groups in biology and I began to use surfing as a vehicle for communicating coral science. That eventually led to Arizona State University recruiting me to join its Hilo-based Center for Global Discovery and Conservation Science in 2021, a position that has since evolved into my current role.

Blending the two disciplines has made my research more creative and my surfing more meaningful. It also taught me the importance of protecting time for the parts of life that keep you grounded. Whether that be surfing, music, art or family, maintaining space for your passions is not a distraction from academic work; it is often the very thing that sustains it.

Here are some guiding principles that have helped me to navigate the worlds of surfing and academia.

The best experiences come when you find a crew that wants to surf the same waves or explore the same questions as you. Some of the most important opportunities in my career came from relationships that started organically, often through time spent in the ocean and local communities, or through a shared curiosity, rather than formal networking.

The researchers, surfers, photographers and conservationists I work with are people who genuinely care about the places we study and the communities connected to them. Over time, those shared values create trust that later opens doors to research projects, publications, funding opportunities and creative collaborations. I’ve found that the best way to find these people is not by chasing status or connections but by consistently showing up in the communities and places that you genuinely care about.

Manchester United must buy Mauricio Pochettino out of his United States contract, even if it comes at an uncomfortable cost

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If there is ever a moment to enact a mid-season managerial change, the November international break is it.

Manchester United do not kick a ball again until November 22, presenting the Old Trafford hierarchy with an uninterrupted fortnight to recalibrate, install fresh ideas, and arrest what has been an alarmingly concerning start to the season.

But, by all accounts, they're not going to take the opportunity.

On the pitch, the case for change has long ceased to be a debate. A return of just one win from ten Premier League matches under Michael Carrick is relegation form and the bottom three is where Man United find themselves.

The team looks passive, confidence is shot, and the trajectory is pointing downwards, even in the face of two improbable Old Trafford comebacks in the space of a week. Despite having a long-admired, elite manager reportedly receptive to an approach, Man United appear set to soldier on with Carrick. The reason, as is so often the case in modern football, may very well come down to money.

According to talkSPORT, Mauricio Pochettino remains open to the prospect of taking over at Old Trafford. The former Tottenham and Chelsea boss has been near the top of Man United’s wish list for nearly a decade, repeatedly identified as an ideal fit throughout the club's post-Sir Alex Ferguson malaise.

The obstacle, however, lies in the United States as Pochettino is contracted to the United States Men’s National Team (USMNT), having recently committed to an extension following their 2026 home World Cup.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Poaching him would require Man United to buy him out of that deal. In 2025, reports claimed that Pochettino’s USMNT contract contained a £20m break clause, a valuation corroborated by ESPN’s reporting that any release fee would sit comfortably in the "tens of millions."

Compounding that outlay is the compensation package that would be due to Carrick and his staff if the club chose to make a change. Less than 12 months ago, Manchester United dismissed Ruben Amorim, whose severance package cost the club an estimated £10m.

Under the scrutiny of the Premier League's Squad Cost Ratio (SCR) rules, and with INEOS tasked with trimming the operational budget, Man United’s hesitation is understandable. However, dressing up Carrick’s stay as an executive structure exercising patience with a long-term project is disingenuous. Sticking with the current coaching setup could easily be seen as a cost-saving exercise.

The danger is that short-term financial caution risks baking in long-term sporting problems. Ducking a payout today protects the club's bottom line, but missing out on European qualification or sliding into a genuine relegation dogfight will end up costing tenfold in lost prize money, reduced commercial clout and squad devaluation.

Pochettino has the authority and Premier League nous to reset Man United, and the November calendar gives them the cleanest possible runway to embed him, at least until the next international break in March, but that is too long into the season to salvage an ailing campaign.

Letting this window pass without making a change in the dugout has the potential to define Manchester United's 2026/27.

Leeds and the Premier League are launching an investigation into racist abuse and threats sent to Jayden Bogle’s family.

Bogle escaped a red card in the win over Tottenham after injuring Mathys Tel, with the Leeds full-back receiving the threats via social media.

Should Jason Bogle have seen red for this challenge? 🟥👀 📺 Stream live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/fuK42Okkcz

His club have revealed they are looking to identify those who sent messages to the 26-year-old, whose family were threatened in one of the posts seen by Telegraph Sport after the 1-0 victory.

Leeds say they are “appalled at the disgusting, racist social-media abuse Jayden Bogle suffered” and will push for punishments to be taken.

The club added in a statement: “Leeds United condemns this behaviour in the strongest possible terms. There is no place for racism in football or society.

“The club will work with the Premier League and relevant authorities to identify the individuals and push for the strongest possible action to be taken against them.

“Jayden has the full and unconditional support of the club and his team-mates, and we all stand with him at this time. Nobody should ever be subjected to racist abuse.”

Daniel Farke, the Leeds head coach, described Bogle as the “softest player” in the Premier League who would never try to hurt an opponent.

Referee John Brooks did not issue a yellow card, with VAR Tony Harrington sticking with the on-field decision.

“I’m confirming the on-field decision of no red card. There’s a lack of speed going into the challenge and he’s stepping into the tackle. Confirming a reckless challenge,” Harrington was quoted on the big screen at Elland Road.

Tottenham will make a formal complaint to Pro Ref over the decision not to send off Bogle.

“I haven’t watched the scenes back so I can’t give you a clear opinion, out of the game it looked a handball but the scene with Jayden was not too far away from my bench and it looked a very unlucky coming together,” Farke said.

“Fingers crossed for Mathys that he is back soon, but it looked like there was not much speed in this action, but Jayden Bogle is one of the most fair players in the country, he would never injure or foul a player on purpose because he is such a fair character.”

Tottenham Hotspur’s purple patch of form ended with a worrying loss. Wearing their “Spurple” kit for the first time, Roberto De Zerbi highlighted a lack of character and personality from his players and refused to blame the defeat on referee John Brooks’s decision not to dismiss Jayden Bogle for leaving one of his players injured.

Spurs’ away strip is based on a 1990s design, but this performance was more Christian Gross than Jürgen Klinsmann or David Ginola. Leeds United created the better chances and eventually broke through with 11 minutes remaining when their substitutes combined for Noah Okafor to score the winning goal.

Noah Okafor came off the bench and broke the deadlock just minutes later ⛓️‍💥 What a finish 🎯 📺 Stream live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/pnbTQM1YpM

After victories against Coventry City, Chelsea and Crystal Palace, this was a blow for De Zerbi after looking to move Spurs into the European places. Leeds had not scored in 298 minutes of football, nor had they won in five previous matches, yet the Tottenham manager could barely recognise the players who had won three matches in a row.

De Zerbi had warned his team they would face a hostile atmosphere at Elland Road, but instead of rising to the challenge, Spurs were passive until it was too late.

“We didn’t win any duels, we didn’t win any one-to-ones, there was space to play and we didn’t take the right position,” De Zerbi said. “We didn’t show personality, we didn’t show what we are or who we are. It is part of the journey for sure. It can be normal in football but we have to be honest, if you are not honest the future is not good. If you analyse our behaviour we can become a top team.

“We worked very hard this week. We spoke all the days about the intensity, the type of game we would have found in this stadium and the atmosphere, it was not a surprise for us. Sometimes it can happen that we didn’t play the kind of game we want.”

De Zerbi’s honesty shines a light on the amount of work that still needs to be done at Spurs. Even after three straight wins, he has refused to get carried away despite fans looking upwards towards the European places.

Neither did the Italian want to blame the officials for failing to send off Bogle. Brooks has history with Spurs, sending off Xavi Simons against Liverpool last season. Here, he booked De Zerbi for his protests after Bogle’s heavy challenge that forced Mathys Tel off through injury.

Bogle trod on his opponent’s foot before clattering into his knee, forcing the French forward off a few minutes later. “I know that Jayden doesn’t foul out of bad intentions, he is not a nasty player and is one of the softest players in the whole league,” Leeds head coach Daniel Farke said. “I call him my butterfly.”

De Zerbi admitted the injury was “bad” and that Tel would now be scanned to determine the extent of the problem. The Spurs boss was upset that Pedro Porro was later booked for a similar challenge, while Bogle went unpunished – but he said the referee was not the cause of the defeat.

“I was surprised because in the same position in the second half there were two different fouls, the yellow card for Pedro Porro is not possible. I don’t know if it is a red card or not on Mathys Tel but the parameter of the referee was not good enough for this in both situations,” De Zerbi said.

Okafor was only on the pitch for 97 seconds before he finished off a move made by Farke’s replacements. Half-time substitute Melvin Bard sent a throw-in to Harry Wilson, who had also just come on and Okafor did the rest, bursting past Rodrigo Bentancur and planting his finish into the bottom corner. It meant the home fans were singing their “I Predict A Riot” winning anthem for just the second time this season.

For Leeds, moving into the top half will lift their own hopes of challenging for Europe, such is the congested mid-table.

“For us it has been a difficult period, we are missing key players like Anton Stach, Noah, Dominic [Calvert-Lewin] has not had the easiest spell with several injury problems and it was important to show this unity and commitment to avoid all their individual quality to score goals and reduce them to very little,” Farke added.

“Our final third, the quality was perhaps not there but second half there was no doubt just one team was pushing for that win. Another clean sheet another terrific defensive behaviour.”

Archie Gray will make his first appearance against his old club today after joining Spurs from Leeds in 2024. He was an unused sub in the two matches last season but is now an established part of this De Zerbi resurgence, starting all but two matches in the current campaign. Gray was named in the England Under-21 squad yesterday but is heading in the right direction for a senior call-up.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin is starting for Leeds today, after doubts over a foot issue heading into the Elland Road fixture. He was named in the England squad yesterday, which suggested he was not ruled out of this clash against Spurs

Roberto De Zerbi has kept a settled team as he looks to make it four Premier League wins in a row. Dominic Solanke is dropped to the bench in his only change, with Pedro Porro coming in – so it may be Omar Marmoush playing as a central forward.

There are many processes in [Tottenham’s] build-up. You need players to interpret this and the legs to cover the centre of the game. It is always complicated [tactically against a De Zerbi team], very dominant in possession. You have to find solutions to be competitive in this area.

The most important thing is what happens on the pitch but [we have bought] Sean [in because of the] tactical aspect. He is sop smart, has experience and also the legs to compete. It’s necessary to have a third midfielder on the pitch to control their processes. On the other hand he is sharp on the offensive actions, many times. Lukas [Nmecha] brings the greediness, physicality and can take the attention off Dominic. he has been very sharp in training, scoring many goals and for that he has the chance to shine today.

Dominic is a key player and thank God he was able to join us in team training yesterday. Overall he is in a good position.

You will always have spells in the Premier League when you cannot convert good performances into results or when you can’t score many goals. We are struggling with injuries for key players in our attack – Noah Okafor, Anton Stach – but hopefully we have also turned the corner.

The pre-season, it was clear [he is] a special talent. You recognise the special talent immediately and he doesn’t need to show something special, you understand? Everything that he does and he is one of the special talents.

The next step he has to enjoy, he has to follow the older players, the players with more experience like [Andrew] Robertson, [James] Maddison, Ben Davies and to find the time to play.

It is my responsibility because when you manage young players and sucho big talents like Luca, it is a bigger responsibility for me.

He has to be ready when he goes on the pitch. I think it [does] not depend on the result, he can play from the beginning. Before the Chelsea game, I thought to play with him in the first XI, but in the end you have to find the right moment and for them also.

I think the age is not so important. The most important is the quality, personality, the behaviour on the pitch and the qualities. And Luca has all of these qualities.

Leeds United are heartbroken to learn of the passing of supporter Colin Westby at the age of 68. Colin suffered a medical emergency ahead of our Premier League fixture with Manchester United on Sunday 18 October at Elland Road. After being transferred to hospital, he was placed into a medically induced coma and sadly following a period of unresponsiveness, the decision was made to withdraw life support. Colin was a long-standing Season Ticket Holder at the club, attending matches for over 50 years. The thoughts of everyone at Leeds United are with Colin's family and friends at this sad time. We will pay tribute to Colin in the 68th minute of our next Premier League fixture with Tottenham Hotspur, on Saturday 7 November.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Leeds United and Tottenham Hotspur at Elland Road. The home side, lions at night and mice in the morning, have the unenviable record of 21 top-flight matches with a kick-off time before 3pm without a win. All that extra TV moolah comes in handy but their home ground, a bearpit under the floodlights, is neutered when its denizens are yawning instead of being fired up by social lubricant.

Daniel Farke’s team started the campaign well but are now without a win in five, drawing three matches with teams beneath them in the table – Crystal Palace, Manchester United and Sunderland – and  losing to two above them, Arsenal and Bournemouth. In fairness they played well against the champions for an hour and were deservedly in the lead until Mikel Arteta turnd to his billionaire’s bench and changed the game. At Bournemouth last week they also made a decent start, had a goal disallowed for striking Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s arm and then James Trafford chucked one in.

They never recovered, found themselves increasingly bogged down when trying to unlock a low block and were mugged on the break in added time to lose 2-0. They are a robust side overly reliant on their wing-backs to create chances for their No 9 in the absence of the injured Noah Okafor who was unavailable to train with the team this week because of a groin injury but may be fit enough for the bench.

Spurs, by contrast, are buoyant following three wins on the bounce – over Coventry, Chelsea and Palace, two with clean sheets – that has taken them from 19th to ninth, three places above Leeds. They have won their last three visits to Elland Road, 0-4 under Antonio Conte, which proved to be the last match of Marcelo Bielsa’s glorious spell at the Peacocks, 1-4 under Ryan Mason, which sealed Leeds’ relegation, and 1-2 under Tomas Frank last year by virtue of goals from Mathys Tel and Mohammed Kudus as the home side struggled against their width back in the days before their switch to a back three.

Tel also scored in Spurs’ home game, a 1-1 draw in May, and then kicked Ethan Ampadu in the head to concede the penalty from which Leeds equalised. I wonder what kind of impact he will have today. Incidentally Roberto De Zerbi on his last visit to Leeds when manager of Brighton in 2022-23 had such a strop on the touchline when the home team equalised that he was within a gnat’s whisker of being sent off.

#1094. Dejan Kulusevski reveals he declined knee transplant during 18-month injury absence

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Tottenham attacker spent over a year recovering from a horror knee issue before making his return this season

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Dejan Kulusevski has opened up about the knee injury that kept him on the sidelines for over 18 months and revealed that he turned down a possible knee transplant treatment.

Kulusevski also explained how his recovery weighed heavily on his mind amid fears that he would never play football again.

The 26-year-old missed 526 days of playing time including the entirety of the 2025/26 season after suffering a patella injury during a defeat to Crystal Palace in May 2025.

He also missed the start of the current season but has since returned to action in substitute appearances against Coventry, Palace and Leeds United.

Speaking of his injury and the extent of his recovery, Kulusevski explored how he thought “it’s over, it’s over” when attempting to get back on the pitch and reignite his career before confessing to his mother that his treatment options may not work out.

Now the forward is back and fit enough to feature on a professional level and has been selected for Sweden’s Nations League games this month. Getting on the pitch against Bosnia and Herzegovina or Poland would see Kulusevski make his first international appearance in two years.

The Tottenham man also revealed why his recovery took as long as it did.

“The reason it took so long is that there are people who haven’t even recovered from injuries like this,” he told Swedish outlet Fotbollskanalen.

“I spent the whole summer talking to other doctors about having another operation. It would have been a knee transplant — swapping my knee for someone else’s.

“So I said no: ‘This is what we’ll do: if I’m in pain when I play, I’ll just have to play through the pain.’ I trained and tried to live like a normal person. I trusted that it would work out. So far, I’ve been right.”

Kulusevski went on to add that he was advised by doctors that a knee transplant had a “50/50” chance of setting his recovery back for an extended period of time.

The winger also spoke to former teammates, Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Ivan Perisic, who recommended a doctor in Serbia and Kulusevski praised the work and advise he received.

He added: “He [the doctor] was so sure it would work out. I needed someone by my side who would say to me: ‘Dejan, this is going to be fine.’ So he was important to me.”

Sweden are top of Group B4 in the Nations League and have the chance to secure promotion to League A.

Manchester United could be about to land Jobe Bellingham as their long-term replacement for Bruno Fernandes.

The Red Devils' poor start to the season has been punctuated by the uncertainty surrounding their captain, with Fernandes having fallen out with manager Michael Carrick earlier this season.

Looking to a future beyond the 32-year-old, recent England call-up Bellingham has now emerged as a potential option in the middle for Manchester United.

Fernandes was dropped by Carrick for the match against Bournemouth, following comments made after the Red Devils' 4-1 humbling by Como in the Champions League.

United fans sang Carrick's name after the loss to the Cherries, however, and booed the players – with Fernandes making up with the manager and returning to the starting line-up ever since.

Yet according to Fichajes, the Portuguese is still a target for Atletico Madrid, as they look to take advantage of the situation.

The report names Bellingham as a “gamble” that the club could well take to replace their talismanic playmaker, with the 21-year-old thriving at Borussia Dortmund, just as brother Jude did previously.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Jobe has recently been named in Thomas Tuchel's England squad for the November internationals alongside his elder sibling, who he shares a similar profile with.

Despite Fichajes noting that “there is no evidence of an offer from United” just yet, however, the Red Devils were heavily invested in Jude Bellingham when he was on the move and could well take a similar interest in Jobe.

United offered £30 million for Jude when he was a Birmingham City youngster, as per Sky Sports, only for the player himself to choose the Bundesliga for his own development.

Jobe has had a similar path, moving from Birmingham to Sunderland before making the switch to Signal Iduna Park at the start of last season.

Bellingham is worth €40 million, according to Transfermarkt. Manchester United travel away to Liverpool when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

#1092. USA pull out of U17 World Cup in Qatar over safety concerns

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The US has withdrawn from the tournament due to the risk of armed conflict in the region

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The USA have withdrawn from the Under-17 World Cup in Qatar, which begins in just over a week, citing the risk of conflict in the region.

A letter sent to players from the US Soccer Federation explaining the decision referred to the US state department’s travel advisory for Qatar.

It issued a level three travel advisory last month, a day after Yemen’s Houthi rebels carried out deadly airstrikes on Riyadh’s international airport, warning Americans not to travel to Qatar due to the “risk of armed conflict” and the “potential [for hostilities] to escalate beyond” areas which had already been attacked.

US Soccer’s letter to players reads: “Unfortunately, in light of current circumstances … we are no longer able to participate in the tournament. The wellbeing of our players and staff will always be our top priority.

“Please accept our deepest appreciation for your commitment to US Soccer and our shared disappointment about these circumstances.”

Fifa’s regulations for U17 World Cups state that nations who qualify must take part or be fined around $24,000 for withdrawing within 30 days of the tournament’s start date.

The USA reached the last 32 in the 2025 edition of the U17 World Cup, the first of five intended to be held annually in Qatar.

It had been set to play Group J games against Montenegro, Chile and Algeria. The tournament begins on 19 November and runs until 13 December.

While the tournament is going ahead several other major sporting events slated to take place in the Middle East have been cancelled or postponed due to the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis and the war between the US, Israel and Iran.

Riyadh’s Six Kings Slam, a lucrative tennis exhibition tournament, has been postponed from October to December; the Dakar Rally, also planned to take place in Saudi Arabia in January, will be moved elsewhere; Golf’s Asian Tour has postponed the Saudi International event; the World Rally Championship will not longer visit Saudi Arabia and the cycling Urban World Championships were cancelled.

F1 is pressing ahead with its season-ending races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi but the 2027 Asian Cup, the continental football championship, which had been due to take place in Saudi Arabia in January next year has been postponed by nearly a year.

Liverpool are planning their long-term future in goal, with the Brighton stopper linked

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Liverpool are looking to Bart Verbruggen of Brighton & Hove Albion as their successor in goal to Alisson.

Verbruggen has been in spectacular form for the high-flying Seagulls this season, keeping seven clean sheets in 10 Premier League appearances, with the Sussex outfit finding themselves second in the table – four points ahead of Liverpool.

Such good form means increased interest in some of Brighton's top performers, however, with the Reds turning attentions to the Amex.

Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson is out of contract at the end of the season, with his imperiously high level having perhaps dropped this season with age.

The Brazilian is now 34 and has made a couple of high-profile errors this season – while his comments admitting that he missed Liverpool matches last season “to prepare for the World Cup” have not gone down well with fans.

Now, TEAMtalk have revealed in a report that the Merseysiders have begun to look to the future between the sticks and have identified Verbruggen as a “credible candidate who could provide stability and quality” in taking the No.1 shirt at Anfield.

Alisson was a transformational signing for previous manager Jurgen Klopp in the wake of Loris Karius' two mistakes in the 2018 Champions League final, establishing himself as arguably the best goalkeeper in the Premier League since joining the Reds from Roma on what was an all-time record for a keeper at the time.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Liverpool looked to future-proof the position in 2025 when they swooped for highly-rated Georgian, Giorgi Mamardashvili, but the 26-year-old has struggled to command the same kind of aura as Alisson.

Next summer, manager Andoni Iraola will welcome 18-year-old Lucca Brughmans from Belgian side Genk in a move that could rise to an impressive £30 million – but a need remains for a senior figure to replace their current first-choice in goal.

Verbruggen is said to be happy at Brighton, though there is interest in his services from Real Madrid, too, who are looking to life beyond Thibaut Courtois themselves.

Manager Fabian Hurzeler will not entertain offers for the Dutchman in January, according to the report, with the player himself reiterating that he is fully focused on life on the south coast.

“I don’t know what will happen in the future: no one knows,” Verbruggen stated recently, adding, “All I know is that, at the moment, I’m very happy in Brighton.”

The Seagulls stopper is worth €40 million, according to Transfermarkt. Liverpool face Manchester United when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

#1090. Odegaard winner spares officials from bizarre VAR row

An ultimately routine Arsenal win but, even by the standards of VAR, an utterly bizarre refereeing controversy. Mikel Arteta’s instant simmering fury at being denied a first-half penalty may also have turned into something rather more explosive had Martin Odegaard not later sent the champions six points clear with a ninth win in 10 Premier League games.

The big talking point arose with inadvertent theatre from referee Farai Hallam when Kai Havertz, who was clearly in an offside position, was equally clearly pulled down by Hull City defender Nobel Mendy inside the penalty area. Which came first? The intervention of VAR suggested the latter. But Hallam duly went to check the pitch-side monitor before then announcing the former.

“After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No 32 on Red No 29,” the referee declared. Cue cheers from the home Arsenal crowd. “However…,” he went on. “Red No 29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City.”

#ARSHUL – 42' VAR recommended an on-field review for a potential penalty to Arsenal for a challenge by Mendy on Havertz - but determined that Havertz was in an offside position in the build-up. REF: "After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No.32 on Red No.29. However, Red No.29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City".

It all sounded so decisive that most inside the Emirates instinctively thought the outcome reasonable. But then came a closer look at the rules. And Law 11.2 certainly did seem to support Arteta’s protestations: “In situations where a player in an offside position is moving towards the ball with the intention of playing the ball and is fouled before playing or attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball, the foul is penalised as it has occurred before the offside offence.”

Arteta clearly saw no value after the match in aiming much criticism at Hallam following a fourth 1-0 win in 10 league games, but did still emphasise his surprise at the decision. “What do you think?” he asked one reporter. “I thought offside, but the law says that doesn’t matter,” replied the journalist. “So not offside then,” said Arteta, who stressed that he needs to understand “what is overruling what in the decision-making” after a Premier League statement simply said that Havertz was deemed offside “in the build-up”.

At the very best, it all leaves further confusion and again opens refereeing body Pro Ref to the charge of inconsistency. Fabian Schär, for example, was awarded a penalty for Newcastle against Bournemouth in 2024, despite being in an offside position when his shirt was grabbed by Adam Smith.

Conversely, Dango Ouattara had a penalty overturned for Brentford against Leeds last season after going down under pressure from Gabriel Gudmundsson before being deemed offside. The crucial point seems to be whether the player has actually challenged for the ball at the time of the infringement and, in this case, the answer was surely “no”.

Premier League title triumphs, however, are often forged on forgettable wins in frustrating circumstances and this was ultimately a classic of the genre. With Noni Madueke continuing to step up superbly in the absence of Bukayo Saka, Arsenal’s combination of attacking persistence and defensive resilience was ultimately rewarded by Odegaard’s scrappy 72nd-minute shot. For young players, it was also every bit as educational as the VAR controversy might be for emerging officials.

Madueke’s low shot forced a save by Hull goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis, but Odegaard was somehow first to the rebound, despite being the wrong side of the penalty spot and five yards behind Hull defender John Egan when the ball was struck.

“The way he scores, not the most beautiful, but the most effective,” said Arteta, who said that his team had sometimes tried too hard for a “perfect goal” and should instead be happy with something “more pragmatic”.

It was a well-judged assessment as Arsenal head into the international break with creative deficiencies, but still almost flawless in the cold hard currency of results. Three wins in three days, including at Anfield and in Prague, also underlines a certain champions mentality.

“I need to praise the players,” said Arteta. “It’s been very very demanding; very short time to recover with all the travel. The mentality is incredible. It’s still going to be super difficult. We can improve in a number of areas.”

When it was then put to him that Arsenal have been offside 35 times this season – with Havertz responsible for 15 of those – Arteta acknowledged that “timing” was one element. But, with Havertz targeted by some frustrated fans, he stressed that responsibility was always shared for those split-second moments by the passer and receiver.

He also singled out Madueke, again easily Arsenal’s most creative player, following his surprise omission from Thomas Tuchel’s England squad. “He went away, started to train, he came back and it was a different Noni,” said Arteta, of his reaction to also being out of the Arsenal team earlier in the season. “You could sense that he meant business and he wasn’t going to accept the situation and, since then, I think he’s been incredible.”

An improved showing by Jaissle’s Newcastle, but they will be dissapointed that they failed to see it through after Jacob Murphy scored in the 80th minute.

Arsenal far from their best, but it is another one-goal win in the Premier League. They are now six points clear at the top of the Premier League, and it is 27 points from the first 30 available.

Another save at Craven Cottage, this time from Hornicek to keep out a sweet strike from Sessegnon at the edge of the box. Moments earlier, Dedic brought down Muniz at the edge of the box.

One last change by Arteta: Zubmimendi on for Guimaraes. Madueke could have made the points safe after slick interplay involving Eze and Merino around the edge of the box. Tried to be clever with the finish, the goalkeeper’s save was deflected back towards the goal and it was hacked off the line.

Leno gets down quickly to deny Lewis Hall as Newcastle pour forward in search of the winner.

As good as Murphy’s goal was, Rodrigo Muniz’s finish with the outside of his foot may well be better. Newcastle’s lead was short-lived.

And they have immediately conceded an equaliser, Rodrigo Munoz with a smart close range finish but Newcastle were be mortified with the defending.

Not for the first time Will Osula’s weak hold up play gives the ball back to Fulham but Newcastle had plenty of men back and failed to clear.

Jacob Murphy has scored the goal that some of Newcastle’s earlier good play deserved. Cut inside on to his weaker left foot, and curled a shot beyond Leno from 20 yards.

Newcastle finally have their goal and what a strike it is from Jacob Murphy. A loose pass from Cesar Palacios in midfield gifted possession to the Newcastle winger and he ran forward, cut inside on to his left foot and curled a shot beyond the reach of Leno from 25 yards.

Arsenal’s captain dinks over Tzolakis after Hull’s goalkeeper saved Madueke’s shot. Odeegard was on the move while the defenders were on their heels. Relief at the Emirates, this has been hard work for the champions. Can Hull muster a response?

This is about as dominant as Newcastle have been in a game all season but they have not been able to find a goal from some where. They have just gone close again as Will Osula just fails to reach Amar Dedic’s cross.

Arteta has made another double sub: Hincapie and Eze replace Tzolis and Calafiori, so all change down the left flank. For Hull, Lucas Herrington has replaced the injured Semi Ajayi at the back.

Felt like the cheers for Viktor Gyokeres to replace Kai Havertz were as much a reflection on frustrations with the German as enthusiasm for the Swede. Havertz has struggled today and is far less convincing in this sort of match – when the onus is more on the Arsenal to create – than he was in scoring the winner at Anfield last Sunday.

Specific explanation for Declan Rice’s substitution is unclear – he didn’t look injured – and so perhaps just reflection of risks associated with a third 90 minutes in six days alongside an acknowledgement of quality alternatives on the bench.

Some changes at the Emirates: Cho and Lewie Coyle are replaced by Joe Gelhardt and Brooke Norton-Cuffy.

Arteta with a double sub: Gyokeres and Merino on for Havertz and Rice, which comes as something of a surprise.

Hull’s goalkeeper Tzolakis has just saved with his feet to deny Madueke. A few minutes earlier, Konsa blocked a Cho shot after a threatening Hull break. Still no opening goal.

It has been all Newcastle at the start of the second half and Harvey Barnes has now failed to take a hat-trick of chances. This was the best of the lot, running on to the ball, middle of the area from a perfectly weighted Yoane Wissa pass, he blasted a shot the wrong side of the post.

The second halves at the Emirates and Craven Cottage have kicked off. No changes from Arsenal, Hull, Fulham or Newcastle.

While Kai Havertz was in an offside position when his shirt was pulled, he may not have been active.

The law states: “A player in an offside position is moving towards the ball with the intention of playing the ball and is fouled before playing or attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball, the foul is penalised as it has occurred before the offside offence.”

However, the Premier League match centre does not see it that way.

#ARSHUL – 42' VAR recommended an on-field review for a potential penalty to Arsenal for a challenge by Mendy on Havertz - but determined that Havertz was in an offside position in the build-up. REF: "After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No.32 on Red No.29. However, Red No.29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City".

Frustrating first half for Arsenal, but it was never going to be easy to go again in the Premier League following a Champions League away game and last Sunday’s big win against Liverpool. Hull have also played with confidence and resolve.

Hopefully there will be more action in the second 45 minutes at Craven Cottage and the Emirates.

An odd moment at the Emirates. Referee Farai Hallam was sent to monitor to look at a shirt pull on Kai Havertz in the Hull box. Through his headset, he tells the crowd that a “holding offence” has been committed – cue cheers from the Arsenal fans – before adding “however, the Arsenal player was in an offside position”. So no penalty. It would have been very soft in any case, Havertz was not close to reaching the rebound from a long shot.

Mikel Arteta predictably furious to not get a penalty, even though Havertz was clearly offside before being pulled.

I’ve spotted something else since I was covering Arsenal in 2018. I was gazing up at the boards that circle the top tier where the club mark every trophy that the team has won. There was previously this big gap, of course, from 2005 until 2014 before the cabinet gradually began refilling. But someone has since had a good idea. They have added all the women’s trophies as well, transforming the tally by just the odd 17 during those tricky years of transition and billionaire rivals owners in the men’s game.

Declan Rice has also just had a shot flash wide, but still no clear chances for either team.

Dan Burn thought he had scored from close-range, but Wissa has been penalised for blocking Castagne so the goal was ruled out.

#FULNEW – 33' The referee's call of no goal to Newcastle United was checked and confirmed by VAR – with it deemed that Wissa fouled Castagne in the build-up. AR2: "Defensive foul at the back post. Wissa holding at the back post". REF: "Castagne held back by Wissa. It's a deliberate foul". VAR: "He's clearly holding him - confirming the on-field decision of defensive free-kick. Wissa is clearly making an attempt to hold the Fulham defender. Clear holding offence".

Some controversy here as Newcastle appear to have had a perfectly good goal ruled out for an innocuous looking foul from Yoane Wissa on Timothy Costagne inside the box. Dan Burn was the scorer. Newcastle’s bench are furious. Most of us are just bemused.

Arsenal have largely been on top after Hull’s lively start but clear chances are scarce and Hull’s fans certainly sound increasingly confident. “You’re only here for the Tigers”, they say. To which a rendition of “champions” rings out. On that note, they had a replica of the Premier League trophy outside the Emirates before the match, with fans queuing up to get their photo with it.

The bright start from the visitors has not been maintained and Fulham have been on top for the last few minutes. Lukasz Hornicek just made a full-stretch save to deny Oscar Bobb and there is a sense inside the stadium that the first goal is coming.

Newcastle, as we have seen all too often recently, really struggle to pass through the lines and when the ball makes it out wide it invariably seems to go backwards again.

Although Harvey Barnes has just forced a good save from Leno from a Jacob Murphy cross. It was easily Newcastle’s best move of the match as Wissa and Osula linked up for the first time through the middle.

David Raya to Arsenal’s rescue, plucking Stroud’s shot away from the bottom corner after a Calafiori giveaway. This has been a positive opening 20 minutes from Hull.

Arsenal with a penalty shout, turned down.

Kai Havertz was going away from goal but Nobel Medy hardly subtle with his challenge – arm and leg – on the edge of the area. It would have been what we call soft but the sort of innocuous challenge that very often results in a foul elsewhere on the pitch.

On a self-indulgent note, this is an all-too-rare trip to the Emirates for me. I covered Arsenal for the last decade of the Arsene Wenger era, ending in 2018 and haven’t made many visits since. A few things are already striking: so many familiar faces still among the staff at a club that has always had more of a family feel than most. Outside, and few of the gaps in the middle (or top tier) that became evident during the final Wenger years when many fans clearly lost faith in the team’s title-winning credentials. The atmosphere is a notch up too.

Thiaw heads wide after a well-worked short corner from Newcastle, but the flag is up for offside in any case. Lewis Hall with the cross.

A decent start from Newcastle United against Fulham and you can see clearer patterns of play emerging. The fact that Fulham are constantly looking to build their attacks by playing out from the back has also helped. The home side have had a couple of scares already.

Hull gain some territory in the early exchanges, and win a corner via a long throw. From the set-piece, Egan’s set-piece hit the side-netting. A shot across Arsenal’s bows.

The lack of Mohamed Beloloumi’s creative spark clearly a big blow for Hull against the best defence in the league; a defence that will be further strengthened by the imminent return of William Saliba. Mikel Arteta had decided that Saliba would be better served by playing against Aston Villa for the Under-21s at Boreham Wood tomorrow. Hull have started on the front, though, in the opening minutes

Updates to follow from the Emirates and Craven Cottage. The Last Post was played and there was a minute’s silence as both grounds mark Remembrance Day.

It’s always great to be back home. It’s the last game before the international break so we know the importance of that and the challenges Hull will provide today. We’re super focused, it’s a massive game for us.

With the amount of games we’re playing, we need that freshness. The team has been performing really well, the finishers have been key again and that’s what we have today – start the game really, really strong and if we need to, have the ability to change the game.

Arsenal’s manager says the centre-back will play an Under-21s game tomorrow as the continues his recovery from a back injury.

Arteta says: “In regards to Willy as well, he needs some minutes. Obviously, the Champions League allows you to bring more players into the bench, but we believe that it’s the best thing to do: to play some minutes at the weekend with the Under-21s and then be fully fit for the international break.”

Arsenal are playing very good football, no matter Champions League or Premier League. They are very strong, they control everything not just against us, also other better clubs. But in football, we have a chance. Obviously, they are a big favourite, and we can start to try to create some difficulties for them.

The return of Sean Steur is a positive move from Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle but is it also a sign the German is feeling the pressure of public opinion on Tyneside?

The 18-year-old has looked the best of Newcastle’s summer signings but Newcastle are understandably trying to ease the teenager into things.

Ultimately, though, Steur is the only midfield player who can take possession of the ball under pressure and despite his tender years they have looked a better side with him in it.

There have been widespread calls for Steur to be called back into the side and Jaissle has done just that for a game he could really do with winning coming off the back of four defeats in their last five games.

Malick Thiaw also comes back into the side for Fabian Schar, with Jacob Murphy preferred to Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa starting in place of Joe Willock. I don’t think any of those dropped can have any complaints.

However, the constant chopping and changing betrays the problems Jaissle is facing. Whatever team he sends out is struggling to deliver what he wants, both individually and collectively.

With the international break coming up, Newcastle need a positive result to quieten the negative noise.
